title: Revenue growth management (RGM) in CPG: a practical guide for brands
summary: A practical guide to revenue growth management (RGM) for CPG brands: the five pillars, the data each needs, and where to start without an RGM team.
body_markdown:
Most guides to RGM are written for companies that already have an RGM department. I've written this one for brands that don't, which was me for most of my seven years running Better Nature.


We were the UK's number one tempeh brand by volume, and we still made RGM decisions the way most growing brands do: one promo at a time, in a spreadsheet, usually under pressure from a buyer's deadline. I didn't call it revenue growth management back then. I just knew some of our promotions were costing us money and I couldn't prove which ones.


## What is revenue growth management (RGM) in CPG?


RGM is the practice of using data to decide price, promotions, pack sizes, assortment, and trade terms together, so each sale makes more money. The goal is to grow net revenue and margin as well as volume. Net revenue is what you keep after discounts and trade spend.


These decisions affect each other. A deep promotion can sell more cases and still lose you money, and a new pack size can take sales from your existing pack instead of adding new ones. When each decision sits with a different team, nobody sees the tradeoffs.


According to the pricing software company[Buynomics](https://www.buynomics.com/revenue-growth-management-guide) , many companies have built RGM teams over the past two decades to bring these decisions together across sales, marketing, and finance. The person leading that work is often called a revenue manager or RGM manager, and they own the strategy across every lever.


You'll also come across net revenue management (NRM). Some firms, like Buynomics, use it as another name for RGM. Others, like the software company[Infor](https://www.infor.com/solutions/revenue-growth-management/what-is-revenue-growth-management) , use it for a narrower part: what's left after discounts, trade spend, and other deductions.


## The 5 pillars of RGM


The five pillars of RGM are pricing, trade promotion, price pack architecture, assortment and distribution, and trade terms. The list shifts a little depending on who's writing it.[Simon-Kucher](https://www.simon-kucher.com/en/insights/unlocking-potential-revenue-growth-management) uses four levers, while Buynomics and[o9 Solutions](https://o9solutions.com/articles/what-is-revenue-growth-management) each use five, though not the same five. I've followed o9's list and widened assortment to include distribution, which Buynomics treats as its own lever ("distribution mix").


### Pricing


Pricing is setting your shelf price, and the gap between your price and your competitors' prices, including store brands (private label). It decides how much each unit earns and how many units you sell.


### Trade promotion


Trade promotion is the money you spend with a retailer for a temporary price cut, a display, or a spot in the store's ad. The decision is which promotions to run, in which stores, and whether each one paid back.


This is the pillar that hurt us most at Better Nature. We once ran a deep discount at one of the big UK grocers that moved a lot of packs. Once I'd added up the promo funding and the dip in the weeks after, we'd made almost nothing on it.


### Price pack architecture


Price pack architecture is choosing which pack sizes and formats to sell, and at which prices. Think of a single can, a 4-pack, and a 12-pack, each priced so a shopper can trade up or down and still stay with your brand.


### Assortment and distribution


Assortment and distribution is deciding which products go into which chains and stores, and then checking they get there. A product a chain has agreed to carry can still be missing from a lot of its stores. This pillar sits close to[category management](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/category-management) .


### Trade terms


Trade terms are the financial agreements between you and your retailers and distributors. In o9's list they include listing fees, volume rebates, and promotional funding. They decide how much of the shelf price you keep.


## RGM without a big data team


You don't need an RGM department to get started. You need the data you already receive, in one place.


Start by checking what you have. Most brands selling through distributors receive depletion reports (through VIP or from each distributor), UNFI and KeHE portal data, and sales data from some of their retailers. Distributor depletions are what a distributor sold to stores, which isn't the same as what you shipped to the distributor. If you aren't getting these reports yet, getting them is your first job.


Then I'd work through four steps:


- **Put your data in one place, with one name per store.** Every source names stores differently, so if the names don't match, a store that switches distributor looks like a lost customer.
- **Start with assortment and distribution in chains you already sell to.** Look for stores that carry some of your products but not your best sellers. You can start here because the data for it already arrives every week: which stores bought which products.
- **Check each promotion after it runs.** Compare depletions in the stores that ran it with the weeks before. It's a first read on whether the promo sold more, and it won't tell you on its own whether it made money.
- **Leave pricing and pack architecture for later.** These need data on the whole market and on how shoppers react to price changes, which usually means buying syndicated data and running price tests. That's where you may need a vendor or an analyst.


Those steps cover one pillar properly and give you a first read on a second. That's still RGM, and it's where a brand without a data team can realistically start. The same approach works outside sales too, which I wrote about in[using AI in CPG operations without a data team](https://corvera.ai/blog/ai-in-cpg-operations-without-a-data-team) .


*Two of the five pillars run on data a brand selling through distributors already gets.*


### What this looked like at CLEAN Cause


CLEAN Cause sells organic energy drinks through about thirty DSD distributors, the UNFI and KeHE warehouses, and retailers including Whole Foods and HEB. It doesn't have a dedicated data team. On Corvera, its eight data sources were connected and nearly 8,000 stores were matched across them, so each store has one record.


In August, the sales team dug into one of its larger accounts, a 150-store chain. Working by hand from portal exports, they found that only 2 of their 13 products were reaching the shelf. When they opened the Corvera dashboard, the gap was already flagged, along with the two best-selling products to pitch and the size of the opportunity. Jon Sowers, the VP of Sales, called the buyer, and adding more products to that chain is now on the table.


"We went digging ourselves, but Corvera already mapped out the action plan," Sowers said.


That's the assortment and distribution pillar, run without an RGM team. The same dashboard puts a dollar value on every risk and opportunity it finds. Working from CLEAN Cause's own distributor, portal, and retailer data, it showed $500K of sales at risk and $250K of immediate sales opportunities when the case study was published. You can read the full story in[how CLEAN Cause found the gap](https://corvera.ai/case-studies/clean-cause) .


## Where the data comes from


This covers the data a US brand selling through distributors and retailers usually has. Your own online store, Amazon, and foodservice each have their own data, and I've left them out here.


Source What it tells you Which pillars it feeds


Distributor depletions (VIP for DSD distributors, or direct) What each distributor sold to each store Assortment and distribution, trade promotion


Broadliner portals (UNFI, KeHE) Orders and sales by warehouse and store, each on its own weekly schedule Assortment and distribution, trade promotion


Retailer portals Store-level sales in one chain Assortment and distribution


Syndicated data (SPINS, NielsenIQ, Circana) Category sales and market share across many retailers Pricing, price pack architecture


Your ERP and finance system (for example, NetSuite) Shipments, invoices, and trade spend paid Trade terms, trade promotion


Syndicated data is market data you buy from a vendor like SPINS, NielsenIQ, or Circana. It shows sales and share for a whole category, so you can see how your price compares. It's the main source a growing brand doesn't already get.


Getting the data is the easy part. Joining it is harder, because every source names stores differently and counts sales differently. As the CLEAN Cause case study puts it, a "sale" is "a shipped case in one system and a depleted unit in another." We built our[AI sales agent for CPG brands](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/sales) for exactly this. It connects the feeds, matches every store, and flags gaps inside chains you already sell to.
